species.howToMeasure: Set the crab flat, shell up. Measure straight across the back from the tip of one long side spine to the tip of the other.
identification: Olive-green to brown shell with a long, sharp spine on each side
Bright blue claws; mature females have red-orange claw tips ("painted fingernails")
Last pair of legs flattened into swimming paddles
Males have a narrow T-shaped apron; mature females have a wide, rounded apron
species.habitat: Bays, estuaries, tidal rivers and marsh creeks along the entire U.S. Atlantic and Gulf coasts.
species.funFact: Callinectes sapidus means "savory beautiful swimmer." A blue crab molts more than 20 times on the way to adulthood.

species.howToMeasure: Measure the claw from the tip of the lower, immovable finger straight back to the first joint (the elbow).
identification: Heavy, oval brownish-red body with gray spots
Huge, unequal claws with black tips
Only the claws may be harvested; the crab goes back alive
species.habitat: Rocky bottoms, jetties, seagrass beds and oyster reefs in Florida and the Gulf.
species.funFact: A stone crab can regrow a harvested claw over several molts, which is why only claws are taken.

species.howToMeasure: Measure from the forward edge between the horns over the eyes straight back to the rear edge of the body shell. Florida requires measuring in the water with a gauge.
identification: Two large, forward-curving horns over the eyes
Long spiny antennae and no big claws
Mottled brown-orange shell with cream spots on the tail
species.habitat: Coral reefs, rocky ledges and seagrass in South Florida, the Keys and the Caribbean.
species.funFact: Spiny lobsters migrate in single-file lines of up to 50 animals, each touching the one ahead with its antennae.

species.howToMeasure: Lay the fish flat. Measure from the tip of the snout (mouth closed) to the tip of the tail.
identification: Both eyes on the left side of the body
Large mouth with sharp teeth that reaches past the eyes
Five or more eye-like spots scattered over the brown upper side
species.habitat: Sandy and muddy bottoms of bays, inlets and the nearshore ocean from Massachusetts to Florida.
species.funFact: Flounder hatch with an eye on each side; one eye migrates across the head as they grow.

species.howToMeasure: Lay the fish flat. Measure from the tip of the snout (mouth closed) to the tip of the tail.
identification: Both eyes on the left side of the body
Diffuse dark blotches that do not form distinct eye-spots
Large mouth with sharp teeth
species.habitat: Estuaries, tidal creeks and nearshore waters from North Carolina around Florida to Texas.
species.funFact: Southern flounder tolerate nearly fresh water and are sometimes caught far up coastal rivers.

species.howToMeasure: Measure from the tip of the snout to the tip of the tail, not counting the long filament on the top of the tail.
identification: Stout, dark gray to black body with pale scale centers that form stripes
Long filament on the top lobe of the tail
Large males develop a blue hump on the head
species.habitat: Rocky bottoms, wrecks and reefs from the Gulf of Maine to Florida.
species.funFact: Black sea bass start life as females, and many become males as they grow.

species.howToMeasure: Lay the fish flat. Measure from the tip of the snout (mouth closed) to the tip of the tail with the tail lobes pinched together.
identification: Seven or eight dark horizontal stripes on silvery sides
Two separate dorsal fins
Large mouth with a jutting lower jaw
species.habitat: Coastal waters, bays and rivers from Canada to North Carolina; spawns in fresh water.
species.funFact: Stripers live in salt water and run up rivers like the Hudson and Delaware to spawn.

species.howToMeasure: Lay the fish flat. Measure from the tip of the snout (mouth closed) to the tip of the tail.
identification: Blue-green back fading to silver sides
Large mouth with razor-sharp triangular teeth
Dark blotch at the base of the pectoral fin
species.habitat: Open coastal waters, inlets and surf; migrates along the U.S. East Coast.
species.funFact: Feeding schools of bluefish can drive baitfish right onto the beach during a blitz.

species.howToMeasure: Lay the fish flat. Measure from the tip of the snout (mouth closed) to the tip of the tail.
identification: Thick, blackish-brown body with a blunt head
Thick rubbery lips and strong crushing teeth
Large males have a white chin
species.habitat: Rocky structure, jetties, wrecks and bridge pilings from Nova Scotia to South Carolina.
species.funFact: Tautog sleep at night wedged into rocks and can live more than 30 years.

species.howToMeasure: Lay the fish flat. Measure from the tip of the snout (mouth closed) to the tip of the tail.
identification: Both eyes on the right side of the body
Small mouth that does not reach the eye
Thick, smooth, reddish-brown to dark upper side
species.habitat: Shallow muddy and sandy bays from Labrador to Georgia; moves inshore in winter to spawn.
species.funFact: Winter flounder make an antifreeze protein that lets them survive near-freezing water.

species.howToMeasure: Lay the fish flat. Measure from the tip of the snout (mouth closed) to the tip of the tail.
identification: Deep, flat silvery body with faint blue lines
Steep forehead and small mouth
Large, firm scales
species.habitat: Hard and sandy bottoms near structure from Massachusetts to North Carolina.
species.funFact: Scup can live about 20 years and school offshore in winter.

species.howToMeasure: Lay the fish flat. Measure from the tip of the snout (mouth closed) to the tip of the tail.
identification: Dark olive back with small dark spots in wavy lines
Two large canine teeth in the upper jaw
Yellowish fins
species.habitat: Bays, estuaries and the nearshore ocean from Nova Scotia to Florida.
species.funFact: The name comes from their delicate mouth, which tears easily, not from a weak fight.

species.howToMeasure: Lay the fish flat. Measure from the tip of the snout (mouth closed) to the tip of the tail.
identification: Pink-red stripe along the side
Small black spots on the back, sides and tail
Squarish, spotted tail
species.habitat: Cold, clear streams, rivers and lakes; New Jersey stocks them every spring.
species.funFact: Rainbow trout that migrate to the ocean are called steelhead.

species.howToMeasure: Lay the fish flat. Measure from the tip of the snout (mouth closed) to the tip of the tail.
identification: Copper-bronze body
One or more black spots near the base of the tail
No chin barbels (black drum have them)
species.habitat: Shallow flats, marshes, inlets and beaches from Massachusetts to Mexico.
species.funFact: The tail spot may trick predators into striking the tail instead of the head.

species.howToMeasure: Lay the fish flat. Measure from the tip of the snout (mouth closed) to the tip of the tail.
identification: Silver-gray body with round black spots on the back, dorsal fins and tail
One or two prominent canine teeth in the upper jaw
No spots on the belly
species.habitat: Seagrass flats, estuaries and tidal creeks from New York to Mexico.
species.funFact: Males croak with special muscles to attract mates.

species.howToMeasure: Lay the fish flat. Measure from the tip of the snout (mouth closed) to the tip of the tail with the tail lobes pinched together.
identification: Bold black lateral line running all the way to the tail
Sloping forehead and jutting lower jaw
Yellowish fins
species.habitat: Mangroves, inlets, beaches and canals of South and Central Florida.
species.funFact: Snook can change from male to female as they grow.

species.howToMeasure: Lay the fish flat. Measure from the tip of the snout (mouth closed) to the tip of the tail.
identification: Five or six bold black vertical bars on a silver body
Human-like front teeth and molars for crushing barnacles
Sharp, stout dorsal spines
species.habitat: Docks, bridges, jetties and oyster bars from Nova Scotia to Brazil.
species.funFact: Their teeth look remarkably human and crunch through crabs, barnacles and oysters.

species.howToMeasure: Lay the fish flat. Measure from the tip of the snout (mouth closed) to the tip of the tail.
identification: Gray to reddish-brown body
Dark band through the eye on young fish
Two prominent canine teeth in the upper jaw
species.habitat: Mangroves, docks, seawalls and reefs throughout Florida.
species.funFact: Juveniles grow up in mangroves and seagrass before moving out to reefs.
